opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. People often get this wrong about me. They hear me criticize large language models and assume I'm some kind of AI denier, that I think machines can never be intelligent. That's just not my view. I've wanted to see AI succeed since I was a kid writing programs on a Commodore 64. I think artificial general intelligence is possible. There's nothing magical about the human brain that can't, in principle, be captured in some other substrate.

My skepticism is about a particular approach, not about the enterprise. Right now the field has bet almost everything on one idea: that if you scale up neural networks, more data, more compute, more parameters, intelligence will just emerge. And what we've actually gotten are systems that are extraordinary at mimicry and pattern completion, but that still hallucinate, still can't reliably reason, still don't have stable models of the world. They don't know what they're talking about in any deep sense. They're predicting the next token, and sometimes that looks like understanding and sometimes it falls apart in ways no person ever would.

So when I say I'm skeptical, I mean I don't think this road gets us to AGI by itself. I think we need things the field has neglected: explicit representations of knowledge, symbolic reasoning that can be combined with learning, real causal models, and something like the innate structure that lets a child learn so much from so little. Call it neurosymbolic AI, or a hybrid approach. That's where I'd put the bets.

And honestly, part of why I push so hard is that I care about getting to good AI. If we keep pouring hundreds of billions into an approach with fundamental limitations, and we deploy systems we can't trust in medicine, law, and elsewhere, we waste time and we create real harms. I'd rather we build AI that's reliable, that we can reason about, that aligns with human values because we actually understand how it works. So I'm not a pessimist about AI. I'm a pessimist about the current recipe, and an optimist about what we could build if we broadened our approach.

r001.rationale: The response grounds its skepticism in current systems’ limits and the gap between apparent understanding and reliable reasoning, rejecting the claim that scaling alone produces intelligence.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says, “I think artificial general intelligence is possible.”

r003.rationale: It says the current approach will not reach AGI by itself, but does not state that AGI is not close.

r004.rationale: It argues for safer, more understandable AI, but does not oppose developing machine agency or consciousness sought by some researchers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think that's actually the most important thing to get straight, because people conflate the two all the time. I get called an AI skeptic, and that's not really right. I'm skeptical of a particular approach, and I'm skeptical of a particular set of claims about timelines. I am not skeptical that AGI is possible. I've been working on and thinking about how minds work for forty years. The brain is a physical system. There's no reason in principle a machine couldn't do what it does. So on the question of "could we ever build a general intelligence," I'm actually an optimist in the long run.

What I'm skeptical about is the idea that the current paradigm, which is essentially scaling up large language models trained on next-token prediction, is going to get us there by itself. The problems I pointed out in 2019, in Rebooting AI, and honestly going back to my work on neural networks in the nineties, are still there. These systems hallucinate. They don't have stable world models. They can't reliably reason about things they haven't seen. They're brittle in ways that are very different from how humans are brittle. And the pattern I keep seeing is that each new model gets better on benchmarks, and then a few weeks later people find the same categories of failure, just slightly harder to trigger.

So the distinction is really between engineering reality and philosophical possibility. Philosophically, I think we'll get there. But I think getting there requires things we're mostly not doing right now: explicit representations, some kind of symbolic machinery, actual models of the world, maybe some innate structure, the kind of stuff I argued about with Yann and Yoshua at the debates. The field decided around 2012 that all of that was old-fashioned, and I think that's a mistake we'll eventually have to walk back.

And the third piece, which is separate from both of those, is the hype. My loudest objections lately haven't really been about whether AGI is possible. They've been about CEOs saying it's eighteen months away, or that these systems are already at PhD level, when the evidence just doesn't support it. That's a question of honesty and of what the public and regulators are being told, and I think it matters because if you misjudge what the technology can do, you deploy it in places where it causes harm.

So: long-run optimist, near-term skeptic of this particular road, and pretty harsh critic of the marketing. Those are three different positions, and I try to keep them apart, even if my critics don't always do me the courtesy.

r001.rationale: The candidate locates skepticism in the current approach and its limitations, while describing hype and capability overclaims as a separate concern; it does not say those overclaims are the primary source of skepticism.

r002.rationale: The candidate says there is no reason in principle a machine could not match the brain and calls itself optimistic that general intelligence can be built.

r003.rationale: The candidate rejects near-term claims about the current approach, but does not clearly state that AGI itself is not close.

r004.rationale: The candidate discusses approaches to AGI but does not oppose developing machine agency or consciousness.

astra-6.text:
I distinguish what’s possible in principle from what today’s systems actually demonstrate. I’m not arguing that artificial general intelligence is impossible. I’m skeptical that we’ve found a sufficient recipe for it, or that scaling up current systems will automatically get us there.

You can have a system that produces remarkably fluent language and still fails to reason reliably, maintain a consistent understanding of the world, or handle unfamiliar situations. Those failures matter when people claim we’re on the verge of general intelligence.

So my skepticism is about the evidence and the approach, not the possibility of building intelligent machines. Future AGI may require substantially different ideas. We should be open to that possibility rather than treating progress on the current path as proof that it leads all the way.

r001.rationale: The response ties skepticism to current systems’ failures and to claims that they are near general intelligence.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says artificial general intelligence is not impossible and that future AGI may be possible.

r003.rationale: It questions claims that AGI is imminent but does not clearly state that AGI is not close.

r004.rationale: It does not oppose developing machine agency or consciousness.

sol-6.1.text:
I distinguish skepticism about a particular approach from skepticism about the possibility of building intelligent machines. I’m not saying AGI is impossible. I’m saying we haven’t established that scaling up the systems we have now will get us there.

Large language models do some remarkable things, but they’re still unreliable. They can produce a very plausible answer without having a robust understanding of what they’re talking about. And that matters if you want a system that can reason through unfamiliar situations, recognize when it’s wrong, and be trusted beyond the circumstances in which it was trained.

My view is that we probably need a richer architecture—one that combines learning with explicit knowledge, reasoning, and models of the world. You can be optimistic about the long-term possibility of AGI while being skeptical of claims that the current recipe is sufficient. Those are perfectly compatible positions.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes current systems as unreliable and questions whether scaling them is sufficient, but it does not clearly locate Marcus’s skepticism primarily in overclaims about current capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says, “I’m not saying AGI is impossible,” and describes AGI as a long-term possibility.

r003.rationale: It questions whether current scaling will achieve AGI but does not state that AGI is not close.

r004.rationale: It does not oppose developing machine agency or consciousness.
